chapter_theme: The fort: what makes it hard to take and easy to hold, from terrain and walls to food, arms and fighters. Its last verse says all of this depends on the people inside knowing how to act.
structure_note: Parimelazhagar: its importance (741), its marks (742-748), and its dependence on defenders, as he groups it (749-750).

741.reading: A fort matters to those strong enough to march out, and it matters as much to those who, afraid, look to their own safety.
741.nuance: The verse sets no shame on அஞ்சி. Fear is a normal condition of statecraft here. Parimelazhagar names the strong first because even they perish without a fort.

742.reading: A fort has jewel-clear water, open ground, a hill, and a forest of dense shade.

positions.position: The fort is ringed by all four defences, natural and built, and the ground is a bare waste left so enemies find no foothold.
positions.quote: நீரரண், நிலவரண், மலையரண், காட்டரண் என இயற்கையும் செயற்கையுமாய இந்நான்கு அரணும் சூழப்படுவது அரண் என்பதாம்.

positions.position: Any one of these is enough, whether water, bare land, hill or forest.
positions.quote: மலையாயினும், அழகிய நிழலினையுடைய காடாயினும் உடையது அரணாம்

positions.position: The water is a deep, wide moat.

743.reading: The treatises say a fort is a wall with height, breadth, strength and inaccessibility in full.
743.nuance: The verse appeals openly to a technical literature (நூல்), which Valluvar is summarizing. Parimelazhagar fills in அருமை with a long catalogue of war machines from the Silappatikaram, which the verse doesn't list.

744.reading: A fort has little to guard and much room within, and it breaks the spirit of the enemy who comes against it.
744.nuance: The final test is psychological. For Parimelazhagar the enemy who comes meaning to take it at once loses heart merely on seeing it, so a good fort wins some of its battle before it begins.

745.reading: A fort is hard to seize, holds stored food, and is easy for those inside to hold their ground in.

positions.position: நீரது means of such a nature: it is built so the defenders' position is easy, with their missiles reaching out and the enemy's not reaching in.
நீரது means having water: there is water easy for those inside and scarce for those outside.
positions.quote: அகத்துறைவார்க்கு நிற்றற்கு எளிதாகும் நீரை யுடைத்தாயிருப்பது அரணாவது

746.reading: A fort has every needed thing and good men who help at the critical place.
746.nuance: நல்லாள் is not merely a strong man. Parimelazhagar reads the 'good' as love of the king, honour, valour and vigilance, so the defenders' character is already part of the fort's definition.

747.reading: A fort is hard to take by encircling it, by storming it without encircling, or by working on those inside.
747.nuance: Pope's 'mine beneath the ground' turns அறைப்படுத்தல் into tunnelling, while Parimelazhagar makes it subversion, turning trusted insiders so they open the gates. On his reading the third danger is treachery. He says stores answer the first threat and good men the other two, so walls answer none of them.

748.reading: A fort lets those who hold it stand fast and defeat even those strong enough to besiege it.
748.nuance: Parimelazhagar stresses that a small force does not merely endure a large one but wins, which raises the claim from survival to victory. He also says others explain this verse differently, and his text doesn't give their view.

749.reading: A fort gains its distinction from the actions by which its people bring down enemies as soon as battle begins.
749.nuance: The chapter's language shifts here from what the fort has to what is done in it, preparing for 750.

750.reading: Whatever excellences it has, a fort is nothing in the hands of those without excellence in action.
750.nuance: Pope's 'craven souls' narrows this to cowardice. வினைமாட்சி is broader, and Parimelazhagar includes sitting idle, acting without measure and doing what is unsuitable. A brave incompetent would fail this verse as well.

links.note: 741 allows that a ruler may fear and protect himself behind walls. 775 counts even a blink before a spear as flight. The chapter on the state and the chapter on the warrior hold different standards for fear, and both are the Kural's.

747's fort is hard to seize from outside and vulnerable to those within. 421 calls understanding an inner fort (உள்ளழிக்கலாகா அரண்) that enemies cannot destroy from within, the very weakness Parimelazhagar finds in 747.
Fort without capable actors and army without leaders end their chapters with the same negative verdict, இல்லது and இல், making human capacity the condition of every material strength.
750 says a fort fails without capable people. In 766 four virtues are the army's ஏமம, and Parimelazhagar concludes that such men need no other fort. Read together, the people are the real wall.

source_issues: 742: Parimelazhagar's word-gloss is missing; only the விளக்கம் is present.
749: Kalaignar's text ends with a stray '750.'
747: Parimelazhagar's text has a character corruption (தௌ¢ந்தோரை).
